analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Medicaid work requirements, eligibility limits, and provider tax rules from the 2025 reconciliation law.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with no cosponsors, was referred to two House committees and has had no further action; the Medicaid cuts it would undo remain law.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Medicaid portions of the 2025 reconciliation law (Public Law 119-21, commonly called the One Big Beautiful Bill Act). That law requires many Medicaid expansion adults to work or do community service to keep coverage, restricts federal Medicaid and CHIP payment for people who are not citizens or listed lawful residents starting in fiscal 2027, and limits state Medicaid provider taxes. The bill would erase those changes and restore Medicaid law to what it was before. It has not moved: no cosponsors, no committee action, no vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income Medicaid enrollees, including the expansion population who would otherwise have to meet work or community service requirements, immigrants who would lose eligibility for federally funded Medicaid and CHIP in fiscal 2027, and low-income patients generally, whose coverage and access to providers would be more secure. Rural hospitals, community health centers, and safety-net providers would also benefit because they absorb care for people who lose coverage.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income Medicaid enrollees and safety-net providers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the requirement that Medicaid expansion adults engage in work or community service to qualify for coverage, removing a paperwork and reporting hurdle that causes eligible people to lose coverage [S2].

Restores federal Medicaid and CHIP payment rules that would otherwise be restricted beginning in fiscal 2027 to citizens, lawful permanent residents, and a few other listed lawful categories, keeping coverage available to people outside those categories [S2].
Restores the Medicaid provider tax rules the 2025 law limited beginning in fiscal 2027, preserving a financing tool states use to fund their share of Medicaid [S2].
Repeals chapter 1 of subtitle B of title VII of Public Law 119-21 and restores any law that chapter amended as if it had never been enacted [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal government would bear the cost of the coverage the 2025 law's Medicaid provisions were designed to reduce, since the repealed provisions were a major source of that law's federal savings. States that used provider taxes to finance Medicaid would keep a tool the 2025 law curtailed.

drawbacks.text: The 2025 law's Medicaid provisions were major sources of federal budget savings; repealing them would raise federal spending, and the bill includes no offsetting revenue or cuts [S2] [S3].

Supporters of the original provisions argued work requirements and tighter eligibility rules target benefits to people who are not working or are not lawfully present; this bill rejects those policy choices outright rather than modifying them [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For Medicaid enrollees the benefit is concrete: fewer reporting requirements and no fiscal-2027 eligibility cutoff, which means fewer people losing coverage. The cost is real but different in kind — the repealed provisions were one of the 2025 law's largest sources of federal savings, so repeal means higher federal spending with no offset in the bill. The policy trade-off is coverage versus federal deficit reduction; the bill takes a clear side.

outcome.mechanism: It sits in two House committees — Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means — with no cosponsors, no hearings or markup, and no vote, while the Congress continues.

narrative.text: Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-PA) introduced the bill on June 30, 2026, and it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee and additionally to the Ways and Means Committee [S1] [S3].
The only action taken was the June 30, 2026 introduction and committee referral; no committee consideration, floor action, or vote has occurred [S5].

The bill would repeal chapter 1 of subtitle B of title VII of Public Law 119-21, which CRS describes as containing the Medicaid provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act — work and community service requirements for the Medicaid expansion population, restrictions on federal payment for non-citizens beginning in fiscal 2027, and limits on Medicaid provider taxes beginning in fiscal 2027 [S2] [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not moved, nothing has changed: the 2025 law's Medicaid work requirements, non-citizen payment restrictions, and provider tax limits remain in place, which is the outcome their supporters wanted. Medicaid enrollees who would gain from repeal are no better off so far.

for.name: Rep. Brendan Boyle (D-PA)
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 30, 2026 to repeal the 2025 law's Medicaid provisions

sides.party_line_note: The bill has no cosponsors and no recorded votes or statements in the record, so the partisan shape is undefined, though the provisions it targets passed in 2025 as part of a Republican reconciliation law.

industries.note: Hospitals absorb care for people who lose Medicaid coverage, so repeal of work requirements and eligibility restrictions reduces their uncompensated care burden. But limits on state provider taxes in the 2025 law cut a financing stream some providers help fund; repeal restores it, a net gain for most safety-net hospitals.

Repeal restores the provider tax tool states use to finance their Medicaid share and avoids coverage costs being shifted to states. It also means less federal cost-sharing relief than the 2025 law provided states, so the effect depends on the state.
Fewer enrollees means less premium revenue for insurers that administer Medicaid coverage; repeal would preserve enrollment and revenue. Their interest runs with enrollees' on this bill.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action since its June 2026 referral, the bill is unlikely to advance in this Congress; a majority party that wrote the 2025 Medicaid provisions has no incentive to schedule it, and bills of this kind typically die in committee at the end of the session.
